What Burned Bread Can Reveal

At a site, pottery, tools, and animal bones are easy to recognize as evidence. Charred lumps may look less informative. Similarly,[1] some of those lumps are pieces of bread or other prepared food that became charred before burning away. Carbonization can preserve structures that ordinary decay would destroy.

In the laboratory, researchers first photograph a fragment and look at[2] an exposed surface under magnification. They record several features, the size of pores, the shape of plant cells, and the distribution of grain particles.[3] A scanning microscope can reveal details smaller than those visible through an ordinary lens. Specialists may also compare the cells with reference samples of wheat, barley, millet, or other plants.

The experimental fragments preserve its[4] own patterns of pores and particles. A micrograph alone cannot show exactly how an ancient cook prepared a mixture. [A] Experimental baking gives the team a controlled basis for comparison.[5] [B] Researchers grind known grains to different levels of fineness. [C] They vary the amount of water, kneading, fermentation, and cooking temperature. [D] Finally, they char a small portion of each replica under controls.

Researchers do not expect one replica to match an archaeological fragment in every detail. Instead, combinations of features narrow the range of plausible methods. Nevertheless,[6] large, irregular pores may support the possibility that gas expanded within a fermented dough. The size and arrangement of grain particles can indicate whether the ingredients were ground finely or left coarse. A cluster of fragments from the same hearth sometimes suggest[7] that several foods were prepared together.

Context remains essential. A bread fragment found beside a grinding stone does not, by itself, prove who made it or why. Researchers compare the food with seeds, tools, vessels, and activity areas for the purpose of being able to[8] develop a better-supported interpretation. As laboratory methods improved, archaeologists have become[9] more willing to collect tiny burned fragments instead of treating them as undifferentiated charcoal.

These fragments rarely preserve a complete recipe. Even so, they can show that people selected ingredients, transformed them through several steps, and adjusted their methods to particular circumstances. Burned food matters not because it answers every question about a meal, but because it makes ordinary decisions about preparing and sharing food available for careful study.[10]
